problems.stem: A teacher drafts a family letter about a new AI tutoring tool. Which version best mitigates risk and respects families' right to decide?
options: "We are excited to use an innovative AI tool this year to boost learning."

"Your child's writing will be sent to an AI tutor for feedback. The tool stores submissions for 30 days and does not use them for training. You may opt your child into teacher-only feedback by replying by Friday."
"We use industry-standard, FERPA-aware technology to support instruction."
"The district has approved several tools; details are available on request."
problems.explanation: Risk-mitigating family communication is specific about what data is shared, how long it is kept, and how to opt out, in plain language.

problems.stem: A reviewer annotates a policy memo: "You offer an opt-out, but every alternative you list still requires the same login and uploads the same data. The opt-out is not real." What does this expose?
options: A grammar problem in the opt-out sentence.
A consent defect: a meaningful opt-out must provide a genuinely different option that avoids the risk being declined.
The memo is simply too short.
A missing logo on the letterhead.
problems.explanation: Consent is only meaningful when declining leads to a real alternative; a fake opt-out is a risk, not a mitigation.

problems.stem: A teacher asks BigAL to draft the family AI-policy memo. What is the defensible boundary on using the draft?
options: Send the model's draft as written, since it covers privacy and equity by default.
Use the draft for structure, then verify each factual claim (retention period, training use, opt-out path) against the tool's actual data agreement before sending.
Ask the model to assure families the tool is safe so the letter is reassuring.
Let the model decide which families need the consent form.
problems.explanation: A model can scaffold the memo, but the teacher must verify every data claim against the real agreement, because families rely on its accuracy.

problems.stem: A policy memo is written at a college reading level and only in English, in a school where many families read at a different level or speak other languages. Why does this weaken the consent it seeks, even if every fact is correct?
options: It will take longer for families to read.
Consent obtained from a notice families cannot fully understand is not informed consent, so the equity and consent checks fail.
The memo should always be exactly one page.
Reading level never affects the validity of a consent form.
problems.explanation: Informed consent requires comprehensible communication; accessibility of the notice is part of the equity and consent checks, not a formatting nicety.
